title_en: Zheng Xuefeng and Chen Guoqing v. Jiangsu Provincial People's Hospital — dispute over a medical service contract
keywords_en: Civil; medical service contract dispute; first instance; basic people's court; Jiangsu Province; natural person; legal person; Contract Law; whether change of medical plan constitutes breach of contract; patient's right of choice; whether mental damages are applicable; partially upheld; assisted reproduction; intracytoplasmic sperm injection; in vitro fertilization and embryo transfer; change of medical plan; good faith; contract dispute; service contract; People's Hospital medical service contract dispute
full_text_en:
Zheng Xuefeng and Chen Guoqing v. Jiangsu Provincial People's Hospital
— Dispute over Medical Service Contract

[Ruling Summary]

When a public medical and health service institution performs a medical service contract, altering the medical plan agreed upon by both parties without consent under non-emergency circumstances constitutes an act of failing to perform contractual obligations in accordance with the agreement as stipulated in Article 107 of the Contract Law.

Plaintiffs: Zheng Xuefeng, female, 32 years old, nurse at Nanjing Red Cross Hospital, residing in Nanjing, Jiangsu Province.
Plaintiffs: Chen Guoqing, male, 38 years old, officer of a unit of the Nanjing Military Region of the People's Liberation Army, residing in Nanjing, Jiangsu Province.
Defendant: Jiangsu Provincial People's Hospital. Domicile: Nanjing, Jiangsu Province.
Legal Representative: Huang Jun, President of the Hospital.

The plaintiffs, Zheng Xuefeng and Chen Guoqing, brought an action before the Gulou District People's Court of Nanjing, Jiangsu Province, against the defendant, Jiangsu Provincial People's Hospital (hereinafter referred to as "People's Hospital"), for a dispute over a medical service contract.

The two plaintiffs alleged: Having failed to conceive after seven years of marriage, they sought medical treatment at People's Hospital and agreed with the hospital to undergo assisted reproduction using the "intracytoplasmic sperm injection" technique (hereinafter referred to as the ICSI technique). However, People's Hospital unilaterally changed the treatment technique plan and actually adopted the "in vitro fertilization and embryo transfer" technique (hereinafter referred to as the IVF technique), which resulted in treatment failure. Therefore, pursuant to the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the Contract Law), the Law of the People's Republic of China on the Protection of Consumer Rights and Interests (hereinafter referred to as the Consumer Protection Law), and the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the General Principles of Civil Law), they requested that People's Hospital be ordered to pay double the medical expenses of RMB 25,000, compensation for lost work of RMB 1,392.50, moral damages of RMB 10,000, and to make a public apology.

The defendant People's Hospital argued: Both the IVF technique and the ICSI technique are means of assisted reproduction, each with different indications. There was no explicit agreement between the plaintiffs and the defendant on which technique to adopt. The hospital's decision to use the IVF technique based on the plaintiffs' condition at the time complied with medical routine, and therefore there was no fault in the treatment process. The relationship between the plaintiffs and the defendant was not an ordinary consumer-operator relationship, and the Consumer Protection Law should not apply to this case. The plaintiffs' claim for moral damages based on breach of contract also lacked legal basis.

The Gulou District People's Court of Nanjing found:

The two plaintiffs are spouses who sought medical treatment at People's Hospital due to fertility problems. On September 9, 2002, the plaintiffs and People's Hospital signed the "Agreement and Instructions for Assisted Reproduction Treatment by Test-tube Baby" (hereinafter referred to as the "Agreement and Instructions"). There are multiple treatment techniques for assisted reproduction; IVF and ICSI are both such techniques. The "Agreement and Instructions" did not explicitly specify which technique People's Hospital would adopt for the plaintiffs' treatment. However, the examination fee paid by Zheng Xuefeng was RMB 5,400, which matched the sum of the first three items in the fee schedule for the ICSI technique submitted by People's Hospital, while the corresponding medical procedure for the last item in the ICSI fee schedule had not yet been performed at the time of payment. The litigation representative of People's Hospital also acknowledged during the trial that the hospital had collected medical fees according to the fee schedule for the ICSI technique. The "IVF Ovulation Induction Treatment Record Sheet" dated September 9, 2002, submitted by People's Hospital, also recorded the "planned treatment" as "ICSI." Therefore, although the plaintiffs and the defendant did not have a written agreement on which technique to adopt, a comprehensive analysis of the above evidence allows the inference that the plaintiffs were aware of the existence of two different treatment techniques. Their act of payment should be considered a choice of treatment technique, and the hospital's act of accepting payment should be considered confirmation of the plaintiffs' choice. Thus, it can be presumed that the plaintiffs and the defendant had reached a consensus on using the ICSI technique for assisted reproduction, and People's Hospital was obligated to treat the plaintiffs using the ICSI technique.

On September 25, 2002, Zheng Xuefeng paid an examination fee of RMB 5,400 to People's Hospital. On the same day, People's Hospital performed an oocyte retrieval procedure on Zheng Xuefeng and collected sperm from Chen Guoqing. After observing Chen Guoqing's sperm, the medical staff concluded that the IVF technique was more suitable and proceeded to operate using the IVF technique, but the treatment ultimately failed.

It was further found that the two plaintiffs paid a total of RMB 6,072 (including the aforementioned RMB 5,400) to People's Hospital for examination fees, medical expenses, etc. To promote ovulation, the plaintiffs spent RMB 5,362.05 on purchasing medication outside the hospital. The total of the two amounts is RMB 11,434.05.

The above facts are confirmed by the statements of the plaintiffs and the defendant, medical records, invoices for medical expenses, and other evidence.

The Gulou District People's Court of Nanjing held:

The plaintiffs argued that the Consumer Protection Law should apply to this case. However, the Consumer Protection Law focuses on regulating the conduct of operators to protect the rights and interests of consumers when purchasing, using goods, or receiving services. The "services" referred to in that law are commercial services provided by operators for economic gain. Evidence obtained by the court from the Jiangsu Provincial Health Department indicates that People's Hospital is not a profit-making institution and does not qualify as an operator. People's Hospital provides public medical and health services to the public, not commercial services. Therefore, the Consumer Protection Law should not apply to this case. Since the plaintiffs brought a claim for breach of contract, it is first necessary to determine whether a contractual relationship existed between the parties and whether the contract had taken effect. A medical service contract is formed when a patient requests diagnosis and treatment from a hospital and the hospital accepts the request. In this case, the defendant had already collected medical fees from the plaintiffs, the plaintiffs and the defendant signed the "Agreement and Instructions," and the defendant treated the plaintiffs. Therefore, it should be held that a medical service contract was formed and became effective between the parties.

Article 60 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China provides: "The parties shall fully perform their respective obligations in accordance with the contract. The parties shall abide by the principle of good faith and perform the obligations of notification, assistance, and confidentiality in accordance with the nature and purpose of the contract and the trade practices." A medical service contract aims to treat patients' diseases. The hospital must act with sufficient diligence and a high degree of care. Due to the highly specialized nature of medical practice, the hospital has considerable discretion in performing the contract. However, the hospital and the patient are equal civil subjects in the medical service contract relationship, and the outcome of medical treatment directly affects the patient's body. It would be manifestly unfair to completely disregard the patient's right to choose. In a medical service contract, the hospital has a duty to explain the medical plan, while the patient enjoys a certain right to choose the medical plan. Before implementing a medical plan, the hospital has a duty to fully explain the plan to the patient or their agent, except in emergencies. The patient has the right to fully understand the possible consequences of the medical plan and has the right to choose among medical plans.

Respect for the patient's right to choose should be reflected in situations where more than one treatment plan exists. The hospital should fully explain the pros and cons of the different treatment plans to the patient and choose the treatment plan based on the patient's decision. In this case, there were multiple treatment techniques for assisted reproduction, including ICSI and IVF. The plaintiffs and the defendant had agreed to adopt the ICSI technique. If, during the treatment, the medical staff believed that the plaintiffs' condition was more suitable for the IVF technique, they should, if conditions permitted, explain this to the plaintiffs and seek the plaintiffs' consent for the change in the treatment technique plan. However, the defendant's evidence only proves that the plaintiffs were aware of the change in the treatment technique; it does not prove that the defendant obtained the plaintiffs' consent for the change. Therefore, it should be held that the defendant's conduct constituted a breach of contract and it should bear corresponding liability.

Article 107 of the Contract Law provides: "If a party fails to perform its contractual obligations or performs them in a manner that does not conform to the agreement, it shall bear liability for breach of contract, such as continuing to perform, taking remedial measures, or compensating for losses." In this case, the medical expenses incurred by the plaintiffs in performing the medical service contract constitute their losses. The specific scope includes the examination and medical fees paid to People's Hospital and the expenses for purchasing medication outside the hospital. The defendant shall compensate for these losses. However, the evidence provided by the plaintiffs for lost work consisted only of a certificate from their work units, not evidence that the relevant amounts were not received at the time. Therefore, it should be held that the plaintiffs failed to provide sufficient evidence for their claim for compensation for lost work, and this claim is not supported.

Regarding the plaintiffs' claim for moral damages, since this case is a claim for breach of contract, pursuant to Article 107 and Article 113, Paragraph 1 of the Contract Law, a party that fails to properly perform its contractual obligations shall bear liability for breach of contract, including compensating for losses. The amount of compensation for losses shall be equivalent to the losses caused by the breach, including the benefits obtainable after the performance of the contract, but shall not exceed the losses that the breaching party foresaw or ought to have foreseen at the time of entering into the contract as a possible consequence of the breach. It also does not include moral damages. Therefore, this court does not support the claim for moral damages against the defendant, nor does it support the request for a public apology.

Accordingly, pursuant to Article 10, Paragraph 1, Article 44, Paragraph 1, Article 60, Article 107, Article 113, Paragraph 1 of the Contract Law, and Article 64, Paragraph 1 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the Gulou District People's Court of Nanjing rendered the following judgment on July 18, 2003:

1. The defendant, Jiangsu Provincial People's Hospital, shall, within five days from the date this judgment takes effect, pay the plaintiffs, Zheng Xuefeng and Chen Guoqing, a lump sum of RMB 11,434.05 as compensation for medical expenses.
2. The remaining claims of the plaintiffs, Zheng Xuefeng and Chen Guoqing, are dismissed.

The court acceptance fee for this case is RMB 1,465, of which RMB 995 shall be borne by the two plaintiffs and RMB 470 by the defendant.

After the first-instance judgment was pronounced, Jiangsu Provincial People's Hospital appealed to the Nanjing Intermediate People's Court of Jiangsu Province.

Grounds of appeal by People's Hospital: The first-instance judgment erred in factual findings. The appellant implemented the assisted reproduction technique agreed upon by both parties. The agreement signed by the parties did not contain any provisions regarding the IVF or ICSI techniques. The appellees' method of payment could not support the establishment of an unagreed matter. Moreover, the payment and treatment process indicated that the appellees supported and consented to the implementation of the IVF plan determined by medical principles.

Zheng Xuefeng and Chen Guoqing complied with the first-instance judgment and did not submit a written reply to People's Hospital's grounds of appeal.

The Nanjing Intermediate People's Court, upon review, confirmed the facts found by the first-instance court.

The Nanjing Intermediate People's Court held:

The parties shall fully perform their respective obligations in accordance with the contract. If a party fails to perform its contractual obligations or performs them in a manner that does not conform to the agreement, it shall bear liability for breach of contract, such as continuing to perform, taking remedial measures, or compensating for losses. Although Zheng Xuefeng and Chen Guoqing currently have no direct evidence proving that the parties agreed to adopt the ICSI treatment technique, the payment receipt dated September 25, 2002, submitted by them shows that People's Hospital collected medical fees according to the fee schedule for the ICSI technique. The telephone recording and the letters from Zheng Xuefeng and Chen Guoqing to the Medical Affairs Department of People's Hospital both mention that they originally requested treatment using the ICSI technique. The "IVF Ovulation Induction Treatment Record Sheet" dated September 9, 2002, submitted by People's Hospital, also recorded the planned treatment as ICSI. The above circumstantial evidence corroborates each other and allows the finding that Zheng Xuefeng, Chen Guoqing, and People's Hospital had an oral agreement to use the ICSI technique for assisted reproduction. People's Hospital should fully perform the medical service contract according to the agreement of both parties. When performing a medical service contract, under non-emergency circumstances, if a hospital unilaterally changes the agreed medical plan without the consent of the patient or their agent, this constitutes an act of failing to perform contractual obligations in accordance with the agreement as stipulated in Article 107 of the Contract Law. In this case, during the treatment of Zheng Xuefeng and Chen Guoqing, People's Hospital unilaterally changed the treatment plan without the consent of Zheng Xuefeng and Chen Guoqing, in the absence of any emergency situation requiring rescue or similar circumstances. People's Hospital's conduct constituted a failure to perform contractual obligations in accordance with the agreement, thereby causing losses to the other party to the contract. It shall, according to law, bear liability for compensating losses. The first-instance court's determination regarding the breach of contract and the specific losses was correct, and the judgment rendered based thereon was not improper. The grounds of appeal raised by People's Hospital were insufficient and are therefore not supported.

Accordingly, pursuant to Article 60, Paragraph 1, Article 107 of the Contract Law and Article 153, Paragraph 1, Subparagraph (1) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the Nanjing Intermediate People's Court rendered the following judgment on June 18, 2003:

The appeal is dismissed, and the original judgment is affirmed.

This judgment is final.
